By a 264-161 vote, the House turned down an amendment that would have blocked the Justice Department from prosecuting patients in the 10 states with medical marijuana laws.
See
 Program Notes for the MarijuanaNews World Report June 13, 2005 1/3 Representatives Protect Patients. Hawaii Fed Backs Off. Cannabinoids Stop Cancer. Mental Illness. African Dagga. American Hemp.

A recent poll found that Americans, by a 68-18 percent margin, believe that medical marijuana users should not face federal prosecution.

The poll, conducted June 8-11 by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research, also found that 65 percent of those surveyed favored doctor-prescribed medical marijuana, with 20 percent opposed.
See
 Leakin Bout My G-G-Generation. Leak of AARP Poll On Medical Cannabis Assures Story Will Have Long Legs. Mainstreaming Real Threat To Prohibitionist Party Line.

However, by a 242-182 vote, the House did approve an amendment by John Hostettler, R-Ind., to block the government from carrying out a federal judge's order that a monument on a courthouse lawn in his district representing the Ten Commandments be removed as a violation of the prohibition between church and state.

Have they actually read the Ten Commandments, or do they just worship the stone on which they are engraved. What about Thou Shall NOT kill?
See
 Lies Have Consequences. From Prohibitionist Venom to the Harsh Realities of Life and Death for Patients. Swedish Prohibitionists, Canadian Bureaucracy and DEAland Medical Murder.

Or, what about Thou Shall NOT give false evidence against thy neighbor?
See

The New York Times report on the vote was in a story about the Patriot Act, but at least they reported. The Washington Post seems to have missed it all together.

 Marijuana Prohibition, Media Criticism, Copyrights and the 8th and 9th Commandments.

Meanwhile, in Nuevo Laredo, Mexico
See
 Mexico, the Drugwar and the US National Interest: Never Mind Iraq; We Need To Pay Attention to What We Are Doing to Our Southern Neighbor.

Mexican President Vicente Fox sent troops and federal agents to Nuevo Laredo over the weekend after some 40 municipal police officers ambushed federal agents sent from Mexico City to investigate the murder of Alejandro Dominguez, a respected local businessman who was also president of the local chamber of commerce. He was the town's latest public security chief. Hitmen machine-gunned him to death hours after he took office.  

The army and federal police on Monday suspended the local police force and sent dozens of them to Mexico City to be investigated for alleged links to drug trafficking.
See
 Czar Reports That One Mexican Official Was offered $60 Million Bribe.

The entire local police force was ordered off the streets after city officers engaged in a gun battle with federal investigative police Saturday that left one federal officer seriously wounded. Heavily armed troops rumbled through the city for a second day on Tuesday.

Drug war violence has killed 45 people and set off an armed clash between police.

More than 600 people have been killed in Mexico this year in drugwar violence, supposedly between smugglers from the western state of Sinaloa and the Gulf Cartel, based in Tamaulipas, one of the Mexican states on the Texas border.

32 U.S. citizens have been kidnapped since August. 

Mexican authorities this week disclosed for the first time that 90 soldiers had been killed in drug-related violence since President Vicente Fox took office in December 2000, vowing a war without mercy on Mexico's drug cartels. In addition, at least 65 agents of the Federal Investigative Agency have been killed since it was formed in 2002.

Some died in confrontations with drug dealers on city streets; others crashed in helicopters after traffickers shot them down or disabled them by stringing heavy cables across narrow valleys where opium poppies and marijuana grow.
See
 Now, How the Narks Created Smack in Mexico. Replacing Marijuana With Poppies. The Iron Law of Prohibition Keeps Working, But The Media Don't

In a recent interview, Fox likened Mexico's "explosion of organized crime killing" to the Al Capone era in Chicago. "Let's recall Chicago in the early '20s. I mean it took years to get rid of the mafias, it took years to get rid of organized crime," he said. Actually, all it took was repealing alcohol prohibition.
See
 Mexican Governors Proposal for Legalization Becomes Decriminalization In The New York Times. Meanwhile Canadian Senate Committee Says Something That Sounds Like Legalization But Is Ignored.

Monday, presidential spokesman Ruben Aguilar Valenzuela announced that hundreds of soldiers and federal agents had been ordered into areas hard hit by drugwar violence. He also called on the U.S. to help stop the flow of weapons into Mexico. He said much of the high-powered weaponry and other technology used by the drug cartels is smuggled in from the United States.

Law enforcement officials trace the current violence to the Fox administration's arrests of 15 leaders of billion-dollar criminal organizations. Rivals have tried to move in and violently take over their territory. There have also been bloody battles within cartels, as lieutenants fight to move up the ladder because of new vacancies at the top, Mexican officials said.

Last month, a federal police officer chasing a bulletproof Ford Expedition in the border city of Matamoros was shot and killed by the occupants, who escaped on foot. The vehicle was found to contain four grenades, five AR-15 rifles, three MP5 submachine guns, two telescopes, 11 cell phones and more than 2,000 rounds of ammunition.

One  Mexican observer lamented, There's no change in the amount of drugs available on the street, and you have more violence. The logical question is, What are we doing this for?

Arresting drug traffickers has not reduced the supply of drugs reaching the U.S. from Mexico. Instead, all Mexico has gotten for its effort is more violence and a rapidly rising drug consumption problem.
From 2000, see
 DEAland Border Patrol Seized 500 Tons Of Marijuana at Mexican Border 500 Times Seizures At BC Border. Putting the Canadian Marijuana Supply In Perspective.

Ironically, a handful of visitors from Texas continued to brave the streets of Nuevo Laredo, lured by cheap prescription medications and duty free alcohol. In other words, they come for legal drugs amid violence caused by the prohibition of other drugs, many of which are less dangerous than the ones that are legal. 

(MarijuanaNews note: I have been ranting about this for months.)
